title: New Covenant Prophecy
summary: Jeremiah’s promise of a new covenant names both Israel and Judah and answers their earlier covenant-breaking with renewed relationship: God’s instruction will be written on the heart, the people will know God, and their sin will be forgiven. Ezekiel 36 adds images of cleansing, a new heart, and God’s spirit. In the New Testament, Jesus speaks of a new covenant at the meal before his death, and Paul and Hebrews interpret the language in their own settings. The shared theme is renewal, but each text emphasizes different parts of the promise.
historical_context: Jeremiah 31 places the promise within a vision of restoration and names the houses of Israel and Judah as its recipients. It recalls the covenant made when God brought their ancestors out of Egypt, then explains the need for renewal by saying that the people broke that covenant. Ezekiel 36 also describes the gathering and cleansing of the people. Luke 22, 2 Corinthians 3, and Hebrews 8 show later Christian uses of this language; they should be read as reception of the prophetic promise, not as evidence for Jeremiah’s original setting.
literary_context: Jeremiah’s oracle repeats the covenant formula—God will be their God and they will be God’s people—while contrasting the broken earlier covenant with instruction written on the heart and forgiveness of sin. Ezekiel 36 uses related but distinct images: cleansing water, a new heart, and a new spirit. Luke 22 places new-covenant language over the cup; 2 Corinthians 3 speaks of a ministry of the new covenant; Hebrews 8 quotes Jeremiah at length. These later texts make the prophetic language central to their arguments, each in a different way.
covenantal_significance: The promise addresses a whole people, not only private inward change: Jeremiah names Israel and Judah, and Ezekiel speaks of gathering them and renewing their life with God. The law remains part of the promise, but the people’s relationship to it is transformed; forgiveness and knowledge of God are also central. Later Christian texts connect this hope with Jesus and new-covenant ministry. The cited passages show that connection, while questions about how the promise relates to Israel, the church, and future restoration require more evidence than this summary provides.
canonical_role: New Covenant Prophecy serves as a prophetic anchor, connecting oracle context, canonical development, and related fulfillment or restoration themes.

interpretive_notes.note: Read the oracle first in its own historical setting.
Prophetic speech is covenantal proclamation before it is prediction.
